questions.q: Which of the following is a covalent (network) solid?
questions.explanation: In diamond every carbon atom is joined to four others by covalent bonds throughout the crystal.

questions.q: The smallest repeating portion of a crystal lattice, which generates the whole lattice when repeated in three dimensions, is called the:
questions.explanation: A unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of the lattice.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of an atom in a simple cubic lattice?
questions.explanation: Each atom touches one neighbour along each of the six directions ±x, ±y, ±z.

questions.q: Iron(II) oxide is usually found as Fe₀.₉₅O. This is because:
options: it contains excess iron atoms in interstitial sites
oxide ions are missing and electrons occupy the vacancies
some Fe²⁺ ions are missing and the charge is balanced by some Fe³⁺ ions
some Fe²⁺ ions have moved to interstitial sites
questions.explanation: Metal-deficiency defect: loss of Fe²⁺ is compensated by oxidation of other Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺.

questions.q: Atoms of X form a ccp lattice and atoms of Y occupy all the tetrahedral voids. The formula of the compound is:
questions.explanation: For N atoms of X there are 2N tetrahedral voids, all filled by Y, giving X : Y = 1 : 2.

questions.q: Sodium crystallises in a bcc lattice with edge length 429 pm. Taking the molar mass as 23 g/mol and N_A = 6.022 x 10²³, its density is about:
Define the term 'unit cell'.
questions.answer: A unit cell is the smallest portion of a crystal lattice which, when repeated in all three dimensions, generates the entire lattice.
keyPoints: Smallest repeating unit of the crystal lattice
Repetition in three dimensions builds the crystal
questions.explanation: Unit cells are described by edge lengths and the angles between the edges.

questions.q: How does doping silicon with a group 13 element such as boron produce a p-type semiconductor?
questions.answer: Boron has three valence electrons, so each boron atom in the silicon lattice leaves one bond short of an electron, creating an electron hole. Holes move under an electric field and carry the current, so the semiconductor is called p-type (positive hole).
keyPoints: Boron has one electron fewer than silicon
Conduction is by movement of positive holes
questions.explanation: Group 13 dopants give p-type; group 15 dopants give n-type.

questions.q: Which concentration term does not change with temperature?
questions.explanation: Mole fraction depends only on the amounts of components, not on volume, so it is temperature independent.

questions.q: Soda water is an example of a solution of:
questions.explanation: Soda water is carbon dioxide dissolved in water.

questions.q: What is the unit of the molal elevation constant K_b?
questions.explanation: From ΔT_b = K_b m, K_b = ΔT_b/m, with unit K/(mol kg⁻¹) = K kg mol⁻¹.

questions.q: A solution contains 1 mol of a non-volatile solute and 9 mol of solvent. The relative lowering of vapour pressure is:
questions.explanation: Relative lowering = mole fraction of solute = 1/(1 + 9) = 0.1.

questions.q: 3.0 g of a non-electrolyte is dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution, which shows an osmotic pressure of 0.0821 atm at 300 K. Taking R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the molar mass of the solute is:
Which 0.01 m aqueous solution freezes at the lowest temperature, assuming complete dissociation of the electrolytes?
questions.explanation: Al₂(SO₄)₃ gives 5 ions (i = 5), the most particles, so it has the largest depression in freezing point.

questions.q: Define molarity and write its unit.
questions.answer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per litre of solution. Its unit is mol L⁻¹ (M).
keyPoints: Moles of solute per litre of solution
questions.explanation: Molarity changes with temperature because volume changes.

questions.q: Calculate the molarity of a solution containing 4 g of NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol) in 250 mL of solution.
questions.answer: Moles of NaOH = 4/40 = 0.1 mol. Volume = 0.25 L. Molarity = 0.1/0.25 = 0.4 M.
questions.explanation: Molarity = moles/volume in litres.

questions.q: In an electrolytic cell the cathode carries which charge?
questions.explanation: In an electrolytic cell the cathode is connected to the negative terminal of the source and attracts cations.

questions.q: Conduction of electricity through an electrolytic solution is due to the movement of:
questions.explanation: Electrolytic conduction involves the migration of cations and anions.

questions.q: According to Faraday's first law, the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to:
options: the voltage of the source only
questions.explanation: m = Z x Q, where Q is the charge in coulombs.

questions.q: Given E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, the standard EMF of the cell Cu | Cu²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag is:
What is the EMF at 298 K of the concentration cell Cu | Cu²⁺(0.01 M) || Cu²⁺(1.0 M) | Cu? (Use 2.303RT/F = 0.0592 V)
Limiting molar conductivities (S cm² mol⁻¹): HCl 426.2, NaCl 126.5, CH₃COONa 91.0. The limiting molar conductivity of CH₃COOH is:
questions.explanation: By Kohlrausch's law: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = 426.2 + 91.0 − 126.5 = 390.7 S cm² mol⁻¹.

questions.q: State Faraday's first law of electrolysis.
questions.answer: The amount of substance deposited or liberated at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.
keyPoints: Mass deposited is proportional to the charge passed
questions.explanation: The proportionality constant Z is the electrochemical equivalent.

questions.q: Why does a dry cell become dead after a long time even if it has not been used?
questions.answer: The electrolyte NH₄Cl is acidic and slowly attacks the zinc container, so the zinc casing corrodes and the cell deteriorates even when not in use.
questions.explanation: The side reaction between zinc and the acidic paste continues on the shelf.

questions.q: According to collision theory, a collision produces products only if the colliding molecules have:
options: energy equal to or above the threshold energy and proper orientation
any energy but a head-on orientation
questions.explanation: Both sufficient energy and correct orientation are needed for an effective collision.

questions.q: The order of a reaction is determined:
options: from the coefficients in the balanced equation
from the molecularity of the overall reaction
questions.explanation: Order is an experimental quantity and need not equal the stoichiometric coefficients.

questions.q: If the initial concentration of the reactant in a first-order reaction is doubled, its half-life:
questions.explanation: For first order t½ = 0.693/k, which does not involve the concentration.

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, a plot of ln[A] against time is a straight line with slope:
questions.explanation: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt.

questions.q: In a reaction, doubling [A] with [B] constant makes the rate four times, and doubling [B] with [A] constant doubles the rate. The rate law is:
questions.explanation: The rate is proportional to [A]² and [B]¹.

questions.q: For a first-order reaction, the time required for 99% completion is how many times the time required for 90% completion?
questions.explanation: t₉₀ = (2.303/k) log 10 and t₉₉ = (2.303/k) log 100, so the ratio is 2.

questions.q: Define the rate of a chemical reaction.
questions.answer: The rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. It is usually expressed in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
keyPoints: Change in concentration per unit time
Decrease of reactant or increase of product
questions.explanation: Rate = −Δ[R]/Δt = +Δ[P]/Δt.

questions.q: A plot of ln k against 1/T for a reaction is a straight line with slope −5000 K. Calculate the activation energy (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
questions.answer: Slope = −E_a/R, so E_a = 5000 x 8.314 = 41 570 J/mol ≈ 41.6 kJ/mol.
questions.explanation: The Arrhenius equation gives ln k = ln A − E_a/RT.

questions.q: Finely divided nickel is used as a catalyst in the:
questions.explanation: Vegetable oils are hydrogenated into fats (vanaspati) using nickel.

questions.q: An emulsifying agent is added to an emulsion in order to:
options: increase the size of the droplets
questions.explanation: An emulsifier forms a protective film around droplets and prevents them from merging.

questions.q: Soap molecules form micelles in water:
options: above the critical micelle concentration (and above the Kraft temperature)
questions.explanation: Above the critical micelle concentration soap anions aggregate with their hydrocarbon tails inside.

questions.q: Which of the following is a multimolecular colloid?
questions.explanation: Sulphur sol consists of aggregates of many S₈ molecules; starch and proteins are macromolecular colloids and soap forms associated colloids.

questions.q: The Langmuir adsorption isotherm is based on the assumption that:
options: adsorption takes place in many layers
adsorption is limited to a monolayer on the surface
adsorbed molecules strongly attract each other
questions.explanation: Langmuir assumed a uniform surface with a single layer of adsorbed molecules.

questions.q: With a rise in temperature, the extent of chemisorption generally:
questions.explanation: Chemisorption needs activation energy, so it rises at first, but being exothermic it falls at high temperature.

questions.q: What is a catalyst?
questions.answer: A catalyst is a substance that alters the rate of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change, and is recovered unchanged at the end.
keyPoints: Changes the rate of the reaction
Remains chemically unchanged at the end
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides a different path with lower activation energy.

questions.q: State the Hardy–Schulze rule.
questions.answer: The coagulating power of an electrolyte increases with the charge on the ion that has charge opposite to the colloidal particles. For a negative sol the order is Al³⁺ > Ba²⁺ > Na⁺.
keyPoints: Higher charge on the oppositely charged ion gives greater coagulating power
Example order Al³⁺ > Ba²⁺ > Na⁺ for a negative sol
questions.explanation: Greater charge neutralises the colloidal charge more effectively.

questions.q: Laughing gas is:
questions.explanation: Dinitrogen oxide (nitrous oxide) is called laughing gas.

questions.q: Which noble gas is the most abundant in dry air?
questions.explanation: Argon makes up about 0.93% of air by volume.

questions.q: Which hydrogen halide has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: HF molecules are associated through hydrogen bonds, raising its boiling point above those of HCl, HBr and HI.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of chlorine in HClO₄?
Chlorine reacts with cold dilute sodium hydroxide to form:
questions.explanation: Cl₂ + 2NaOH (cold, dilute) → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O; with hot concentrated NaOH, chlorate forms instead.

questions.q: Among the hydrides of group 15, the one with the lowest boiling point is:
questions.explanation: Boiling points rise from PH₃ to SbH₃, but NH₃ is anomalously high because of hydrogen bonding, so PH₃ is lowest.

questions.q: Name two allotropic forms of sulphur.
questions.explanation: Both consist of S₈ rings but differ in crystal structure; rhombic is the stable form at room temperature.

questions.q: The bond dissociation enthalpy of F₂ is lower than that of Cl₂. Give the reason.
questions.answer: Fluorine atoms are very small, so the lone pairs on the two atoms in F₂ repel each other strongly. This repulsion weakens the F–F bond and lowers its bond dissociation enthalpy.
questions.explanation: The order of bond enthalpy is Cl₂ > Br₂ > F₂ > I₂.

questions.q: In the actinoid series the electrons are progressively filled into the:
questions.explanation: Actinoids (Z = 90–103) are 5f-block elements.

questions.q: The general outer electronic configuration of d-block elements is:
questions.explanation: d-Block elements are filling the (n−1)d orbitals, with one or two electrons in the outer s orbital.

questions.q: The most stable oxidation state of scandium is:
questions.explanation: Loss of 3d¹4s² electrons gives Sc³⁺, which has the noble gas configuration.

questions.q: Potassium dichromate is prepared industrially from the ore:
questions.explanation: Chromite ore is fused with sodium carbonate in air, and the sodium chromate formed is converted to dichromate.

questions.q: Which lanthanoid commonly shows the +4 oxidation state in addition to +3?
questions.explanation: Ce⁴⁺ has the empty 4f⁰ configuration; Eu prefers +2 (4f⁷).

questions.q: Zirconium and hafnium have almost identical atomic radii mainly because of:
questions.explanation: The poor shielding by 4f electrons shrinks Hf so that its size matches that of Zr, making them very hard to separate.

questions.q: What are lanthanoids? Write their general electronic configuration.
questions.answer: Lanthanoids are the 14 elements following lanthanum (Z = 58–71) in which the 4f subshell is progressively filled. General configuration: [Xe] 4f¹⁻¹⁴ 5d⁰⁻¹ 6s².
questions.explanation: They are also called rare-earth elements.

questions.q: Why do transition metals readily form alloys?
questions.answer: Transition metals have similar atomic radii, so atoms of one metal can easily replace atoms of another in the crystal lattice, forming solid solutions called alloys (e.g. brass, steel).
keyPoints: One metal's atoms replace another's in the lattice
questions.explanation: Similar sizes allow substitution without distorting the lattice much.

questions.q: The number of donor atoms of the ligands attached directly to the central metal atom or ion is called its:
questions.explanation: This is the definition of coordination number.

questions.q: In IUPAC names of complexes, NH₃ as a ligand is named:
questions.explanation: Neutral NH₃ is called 'ammine' in complex names.

questions.q: The formula of sodium hexanitrito-N-cobaltate(III) is:
questions.explanation: Co³⁺ + 6 NO₂⁻ gives a 3− complex ion, needing three Na⁺.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds shows linkage isomerism?
questions.explanation: The ambidentate NO₂⁻ ligand is bonded through N in one and through O in the other.

questions.q: What are the coordination number and oxidation state of chromium in K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃]? (oxalate is bidentate)
questions.explanation: Three bidentate oxalates give coordination number 6; 3(+1) + x + 3(−2) = 0 gives x = +3.

questions.q: [Ni(CO)₄] has which hybridisation and shape?
questions.explanation: Ni(0) is effectively d¹⁰; four CO ligands use the 4s and three 4p orbitals, so it is sp³ and tetrahedral (diamagnetic).

questions.q: What is a chelate? Give one example.
questions.answer: A chelate is a complex in which a polydentate (di- or polydentate) ligand binds to the central metal through two or more donor atoms, forming ring structures. Example: [Co(en)₃]³⁺ or the EDTA complex of Ca²⁺.
keyPoints: Polydentate ligand binds through more than one donor atom
questions.explanation: Chelates are more stable than complexes of similar monodentate ligands.

questions.q: Give two limitations of valence bond theory for coordination compounds.
questions.answer: It does not explain the colours of coordination compounds and cannot give a quantitative interpretation of their magnetic data or of thermodynamic and kinetic stabilities; it also does not explain why some complexes are inner-orbital while others are outer-orbital.
keyPoints: Does not explain colour of complexes
No quantitative treatment of magnetic or stability data
questions.explanation: Crystal field theory overcomes these limitations.

questions.q: Chloroform is stored in dark-coloured bottles to prevent its:
options: oxidation by air to poisonous phosgene
questions.explanation: In light and air, chloroform is slowly oxidised to carbonyl chloride (phosgene), which is toxic.

questions.q: The compound CCl₂F₂ is commonly known as:
questions.explanation: CCl₂F₂ is the chlorofluorocarbon known as Freon-12.

questions.q: Which compound has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: For the same alkyl group, boiling point increases with the size and polarisability of the halogen.

questions.q: The reaction of methane with chlorine in sunlight proceeds by:
questions.explanation: UV light splits Cl₂ into chlorine radicals, starting a radical chain substitution.

questions.q: Chlorobenzene heated with aqueous NaOH at about 623 K and 300 atm, followed by acidification, gives:
questions.explanation: Under these drastic conditions the –Cl is replaced by –OH (Dow process), giving phenol.

questions.q: DDT, an insecticide, is chemically:
questions.explanation: DDT stands for dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane; it is a persistent organochlorine compound.

questions.q: Write the IUPAC name of CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃.
questions.explanation: Number the chain from the end that gives the halogen the lowest locant.

questions.q: What is the Swarts reaction? Give an example.
questions.answer: Alkyl chlorides or bromides are heated with a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃ to give alkyl fluorides, e.g. CH₃Br + AgF → CH₃F + AgBr.
keyPoints: Reagent: AgF, Hg₂F₂, CoF₂ or SbF₃
Example such as CH₃Br + AgF → CH₃F + AgBr
questions.explanation: Direct fluorination is too violent, so halogen exchange is used.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂OH?
questions.explanation: A three-carbon chain with –OH on the end carbon is propan-1-ol.

questions.q: Ethanol is oxidised by an excess of acidified potassium dichromate to:
questions.explanation: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to the aldehyde and then to the carboxylic acid by strong oxidising agents.

questions.q: Diethyl ether is obtained by heating excess ethanol with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about:
questions.explanation: At about 413 K the intermolecular dehydration gives ether; at 443 K ethene is formed.

questions.q: Phenol dissolves in aqueous NaOH but not in aqueous NaHCO₃ because:
options: phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid
NaHCO₃ is a stronger base than NaOH
questions.explanation: Phenol is acidic enough to react with a strong base but not with the weak base HCO₃⁻.

questions.q: Which alcohol resists oxidation by mild oxidising agents because it has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the –OH group?
questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols lack an α-hydrogen, so they are not oxidised without breaking C–C bonds.

questions.q: Sodium phenoxide is heated with CO₂ at about 400 K and 4–7 atm, and then acidified. The product is:
questions.explanation: This is the Kolbe reaction, which introduces –COOH at the ortho position of phenol.

questions.q: What is absolute alcohol and how is it obtained from rectified spirit?
questions.answer: Absolute alcohol is practically 100% pure ethanol. It is obtained from rectified spirit (95% ethanol) by azeotropic distillation with benzene, which removes the water.
keyPoints: Rectified spirit is a 95% azeotrope with water
Water is removed by distillation with benzene
questions.explanation: Ordinary distillation cannot remove the last 5% water because of the azeotrope.

questions.q: Why is ethanol completely miscible with water while hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble?
questions.answer: Both form hydrogen bonds with water through –OH, but in hexan-1-ol the large non-polar hydrocarbon chain disrupts the hydrogen bonding of water and outweighs the polar group. Ethanol's short chain has a small non-polar part, so solubility is high.
keyPoints: Solubility falls as the alkyl chain grows
questions.explanation: Solubility reflects the balance of polar and non-polar parts.

questions.q: Which acid is responsible for the pain of an ant sting?
questions.explanation: Methanoic (formic) acid occurs in red ants, hence its name.

questions.q: Which of the following is a ketone?
questions.explanation: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (butanone) has a carbonyl group between two carbon atoms.

questions.q: Reduction of the C=O group to CH₂ using hydrazine and KOH in ethylene glycol is called:
questions.explanation: Wolff–Kishner reduction uses NH₂NH₂/KOH at high temperature in a basic medium.

questions.q: Ethanal reacts with HCN to give:
questions.explanation: HCN adds across the C=O bond: CH₃CHO + HCN → CH₃CH(OH)CN.

questions.q: Benzoic acid is treated with Cl₂ in the presence of FeCl₃. The main product is:
options: a mixture of ortho and para isomers
questions.explanation: The –COOH group deactivates the ring and directs the incoming electrophile to the meta position.

questions.q: A compound of formula C₃H₆O reduces Tollens' reagent. It must be:
questions.explanation: Only an aldehyde gives a silver mirror; propanal is the aldehyde with formula C₃H₆O.

questions.q: Write the functional group and the general formula of a carboxylic acid.
questions.answer: The functional group is the carboxyl group, –COOH. For saturated monocarboxylic acids the general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH (or R–COOH).
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group combines a carbonyl and a hydroxyl group.

questions.q: How is benzoic acid prepared from toluene?
questions.answer: Toluene is oxidised by heating with alkaline KMnO₄ (or acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇); the side-chain –CH₃ is oxidised to –COOH, and acidification liberates benzoic acid.
keyPoints: Oxidation of the side chain of toluene
Reagent: alkaline or acidic KMnO₄ (or K₂Cr₂O₇)
questions.explanation: Any alkyl side chain with a benzylic hydrogen is oxidised to –COOH.

questions.q: How many alkyl groups are attached to the nitrogen atom in a tertiary amine?
questions.explanation: In a tertiary amine all three hydrogens of NH₃ are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

questions.q: Methylamine at room temperature is a:
questions.explanation: The lowest members of the aliphatic amines, such as methylamine, are gases with a fishy smell.

questions.q: Aniline can be prepared from nitrobenzene by:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen over a palladium or nickel catalyst reduces the nitro group to an amino group.

questions.q: Aniline reacts with acetic anhydride to give:
questions.explanation: Acetylation of the –NH₂ group gives N-phenylethanamide (acetanilide).

questions.q: Which of the following is the weakest base?
questions.explanation: The –NO₂ group withdraws electrons and further lowers the availability of the lone pair on nitrogen.

questions.q: Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with CuCN (Sandmeyer reaction) to give:
questions.explanation: The diazonium group is replaced by –CN, giving C₆H₅CN.

questions.q: Define primary, secondary and tertiary amines with one example each.
questions.answer: A primary amine has one alkyl/aryl group on nitrogen (CH₃NH₂), a secondary amine has two (CH₃NHCH₃) and a tertiary amine has three ((CH₃)₃N).
questions.explanation: Classification depends on the number of hydrogens of NH₃ replaced.

questions.q: Why do primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines of comparable molar mass?
questions.answer: Primary amines have two N–H bonds and form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Tertiary amines have no N–H bond and so cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, so their boiling points are lower.
keyPoints: Primary amines have N–H and hydrogen-bond with each other
Tertiary amines have no N–H bond
Hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point
questions.explanation: The order of boiling points is primary > secondary > tertiary.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disaccharide?
questions.explanation: Lactose is composed of galactose and glucose units.

questions.q: Vitamin K is needed for:
questions.explanation: Vitamin K helps in the synthesis of prothrombin, needed for blood clotting.

questions.q: Which common α-amino acid is optically inactive?
questions.explanation: In glycine the α-carbon carries two hydrogens, so it is not chiral.

questions.q: Starch is hydrolysed to maltose by the enzyme:
questions.explanation: Amylase (diastase) breaks starch into maltose; maltase then gives glucose.

questions.q: In protein synthesis, which nucleic acid carries amino acids to the ribosome?
questions.explanation: Transfer RNA (tRNA) binds specific amino acids and delivers them according to the codons of mRNA.

questions.q: Complete hydrolysis of DNA gives:
options: phosphoric acid, ribose and the bases A, G, C and U
amino acids and phosphoric acid only
phosphoric acid, deoxyribose and the bases A, G, C and T
questions.explanation: DNA is made of phosphate, 2-deoxyribose and the four bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine.

questions.q: What are enzymes?
questions.answer: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly globular proteins, that speed up specific biochemical reactions in living organisms without being used up.
questions.explanation: Each enzyme acts on a particular substrate.

questions.q: Distinguish between fibrous and globular proteins with one example of each.
questions.answer: Fibrous proteins have long thread-like polypeptide chains held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds; they are insoluble in water (e.g. keratin, myosin). Globular proteins have chains folded into a spherical shape and are usually soluble in water (e.g. insulin, albumin).
keyPoints: Fibrous: thread-like, insoluble in water, e.g. keratin
Globular: spherical, soluble in water, e.g. insulin or albumin
questions.explanation: The shape of the polypeptide chain determines the solubility and function.
